model.name: Digital Signature / Proof
model.purpose: Provide the reusable context a host record needs to state that a digital signature or cryptographic proof exists over given content: under which algorithm and parameter policy it was produced, which signer identity and verification method it references, and what structured verification evidence and outcomes have been recorded about it.
model.scope_statement: A format-neutral mixin attached to any host record or artifact. It carries the signature or proof instance and its binding to covered content, the signer and verification-method reference, the complete signature and digest algorithm declaration with its policy state, the agility and transition posture, and the verification context, evidence references and structured, dimension-separated outcomes. It does not own key or certificate lifecycle, trust-path validation, time-stamping operation, the runtime verification engine, enforcement, audit trails, or the legal determination of a signature's effect; those are referenced, not reproduced.
in_scope: Signature or proof instance: signature value and encoding, container format and profile, and the binding to the exact covered byte sequence and its canonicalisation or transform chain.
Signer and verification-method context: the signer identity claim carried by the proof and the reference to the verification method or key, together with its algorithm binding.

Signature and digest algorithm declaration: registry-scoped identifiers with complete parameter sets, curve or group and key size, digest and output length, context strings and pre-hash mode, plus explicitly recorded parameter ambiguity.
Algorithm policy state: security-strength target, approval, deprecation or disallowance state per named authority, sunset dates, and the policy snapshot pinned at validation time.

Algorithm agility and transition: verifier-side accepted-algorithm sets, downgrade and algorithm-confusion controls, randomized, deterministic or hedged signing profile, hybrid and composite constructions, and post-quantum migration state.
Proof purpose, domain, challenge, and proof set or proof chain relationships as declared by the proof.

Verification context and evidence: inputs consumed, validation time and time basis, claimed signing time versus proof-of-existence references, verifier and tool identity and version, and references to externally produced validation reports.
Structured verification outcomes with machine-readable reason codes, reported separately for each validity dimension.
out_of_scope: Key generation, custody, rotation, escrow and HSM or signature-creation-device lifecycle.
Certificate issuance, revocation publication, trust-anchor stores, trusted lists, and certification-path construction or validation algorithms.
Operation of time-stamping authorities and time-source traceability.
Execution of verification, acceptance or enforcement decisions, and the verifying system's audit trail.
Determination of legal effect, signature qualification and regulatory supervision.
Encryption and confidentiality, and MAC-only integrity without signer attribution.
The host record's own content model, business lifecycle and retention execution.
Definition or maintenance of external algorithm registries and national cryptographic catalogues.

boundary_notes.distinction: This mixin carries a reference to the verification method or key and its algorithm binding as subject-specific parameters. Key generation, custody, rotation, revocation and device assurance stay in the neighbour and are never mirrored here.

boundary_notes.neighbor: Certificate trust-path and revocation validation model
boundary_notes.distinction: Trust-path outcome is recorded here only as one reported dimension with its reason code and the reference to the determination. Path construction, revocation retrieval and trusted-list evaluation are the neighbour's lifecycle.
Time-stamp tokens are referenced as external evidence for signing-time claims and sunset comparison. Token issuance, TSA policy and time traceability belong to the neighbour.

boundary_notes.neighbor: Verification service execution and audit-record model
boundary_notes.distinction: Verifier identity, tool version and validation-report references are recorded as provenance data. Running the verification, deciding acceptance, and maintaining the audit trail are owned by the neighbour.

Qualification and legal effect are recorded as separate reported dimensions carrying a determination reference, jurisdiction and instrument. The determination itself is made under the neighbour's authority.

boundary_notes.neighbor: External algorithm registries and cryptographic policy catalogues
boundary_notes.distinction: Identifiers, approval states and sunset dates are aligned and pinned by reference. This model neither defines nor maintains those catalogues and makes no conformance claim on their behalf.

sources.title: FIPS 186-5, Digital Signature Standard (DSS)
sources.organization: National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST)
sources.relevance: Normative catalogue of approved signature algorithms (RSA, ECDSA, EdDSA), retention of DSA for verification of existing signatures only, and the requirement to pair a signature algorithm with an approved hash function.

sources.title: FIPS 204, Module-Lattice-Based Digital Signature Standard (ML-DSA)
sources.organization: National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST)
sources.relevance: Post-quantum signature standard supplying parameter-set identifiers and the notion of quantum-resistant signature suites that algorithm-policy records must be able to express.

sources.title: NIST SP 800-57 Part 1 Rev. 5, Recommendation for Key Management: Part 1 - General
sources.organization: National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST)
sources.relevance: Source of security-strength framing and of the separation between key-management lifecycle (out of scope here) and the algorithm and key types employed by a signature.

sources.title: NIST SP 800-131A Rev. 2, Transitioning the Use of Cryptographic Algorithms and Key Lengths
sources.organization: National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST)
sources.relevance: Currently final transition guidance: the basis for recording an algorithm's transition status and for distinguishing signature generation from signature verification when assigning that status.

sources.title: NIST SP 800-131A Rev. 3 (Initial Public Draft), Transitioning the Use of Cryptographic Algorithms and Key Lengths
sources.organization: National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST)
sources.relevance: Draft proposing retirement of DSA signature generation and of SHA-1 and 224-bit hash functions, and the move from 112-bit to 128-bit security strength; cited as draft status, not as a conformance target.

sources.title: NIST IR 8547 (Initial Public Draft), Transition to Post-Quantum Cryptography Standards
sources.organization: National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST)
sources.relevance: Draft roadmap for migrating quantum-vulnerable signature algorithms to post-quantum standards; supports a recorded migration-state field pinned to a named policy rather than a universal date.

sources.title: CBOR Object Signing and Encryption (COSE) - COSE Algorithms registry
sources.relevance: Change-controlled registry of numeric algorithm labels with Name, Value, Description, Capabilities, Change Controller, Reference and a Recommended column carrying Yes / No / Deprecated states.

sources.title: JSON Object Signing and Encryption (JOSE) - JSON Web Signature and Encryption Algorithms registry
sources.relevance: Registry of alg names with Implementation Requirements values including Deprecated and Prohibited (for example RS1 and HS1), and an Algorithm Analysis Document column; evidence that identifier state is registry-scoped.

sources.title: RFC 8725 (BCP 225), JSON Web Token Best Current Practices
sources.relevance: Normative basis for verifier-side algorithm allow-lists, one-algorithm-per-key binding, rejection of the none algorithm and mitigation of algorithm-confusion and key-substitution attacks.

sources.title: RFC 6979, Deterministic Usage of the Digital Signature Algorithm (DSA) and Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm (ECDSA)
sources.relevance: Establishes that deterministic signatures remain fully compatible with plain DSA and ECDSA and that verifiers need not be aware of the nonce-derivation process, so randomness mode is not verifier-observable.

sources.title: RFC 5652, Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS)
sources.relevance: Defines signed attributes including signing-time as the time the signer believes the signature was generated, and requires recipients to recompute digests rather than rely on originator-supplied values.

sources.title: RFC 3161, Internet X.509 Public Key Infrastructure Time-Stamp Protocol (TSP)
sources.relevance: Defines the time-stamp token as proof that a datum existed before a particular time, and states the TSA does not examine the imprint; the basis for treating proof of existence as external evidence.

sources.title: ETSI EN 319 102-1 V1.4.1, Electronic Signatures and Trust Infrastructures (ESI); Procedures for Creation and Validation of AdES Digital Signatures; Part 1: Creation and Validation
sources.relevance: Normative validation model: the TOTAL-PASSED / INDETERMINATE / TOTAL-FAILED indications with sub-indications, validation constraints including cryptographic sunset dates, validation time, proof of existence and the basic, long-term and archival validation processes.

sources.title: ETSI TS 119 102-2 V1.4.1, Procedures for Creation and Validation of AdES Digital Signatures; Part 2: Signature Validation Report
sources.relevance: Defines the structure of a signature validation report, including validation objects used (trust anchors, revocation data, time-stamps) and a signature over the report, enabling inspection of the causes behind a status indication.

sources.title: ETSI TS 119 312 V2.1.1, Electronic Signatures and Trust Infrastructures (ESI); Cryptographic Suites
sources.relevance: Defines a cryptographic signature suite as the combination of message-encoding function, hash function and signature scheme, and acts as the European algorithm-policy catalogue that a policy pin can cite.

sources.title: Verifiable Credential Data Integrity 1.0
sources.relevance: Defines proof properties (type, cryptosuite, created, expires, verificationMethod, proofPurpose, proofValue, domain, challenge, nonce, previousProof), proof sets and chains, and a verification result carrying verified, errors and warnings.

sources.title: Composite Module-Lattice-Based Digital Signature Algorithm (ML-DSA) for use in X.509 Public Key Infrastructure (draft-ietf-lamps-pq-composite-sigs)
sources.relevance: Defines composite algorithm identifiers and the rule that a valid result is output if and only if all component signatures validate, plus the EUF-CMA versus SUF-CMA security-property caveat; cited as draft.

sources.title: Digital Signature Service (DSS) documentation - eSignature building block
sources.relevance: Public-authority description of the ETSI validation model as implemented: the enumerated sub-indications, cryptographic constraints with algorithm sunset dates, and the separation of signature qualification from signature validation.

bundles.name: Algorithm and parameter policy binding
bundles.description: The context that fixes exactly which cryptographic suite a signature or proof uses, what policy state that suite holds, and how the record behaves under agility, downgrade pressure and post-quantum transition.
bundles.rationale: Signature semantics are undecidable without a complete, unambiguous suite declaration and the policy under which it was judged. NIST fixes approved algorithms and transition status, IANA registries fix identifier scope and state values, and ETSI fixes the cryptographic-constraint and sunset model, so this concern is separable from the verification episode that consumes it.

layers.name: Suite declaration and policy state
layers.description: Identification of the signature and digest algorithms with their complete parameter sets, and the approval state, security strength and pinned policy under which those parameters were assessed.

findings.name: Signature and digest suite identification with parameter completeness
findings.description: Records the signature and digest algorithm identifiers together with the registry namespace they belong to and the full parameter set needed to reproduce verification: scheme and encoding or padding, curve or group, modulus or key size, digest function and output length, pre-hash mode and any context or domain-separation string. Absent, inherited or ambiguous parameters are recorded as an explicit completeness status rather than silently defaulted.

questions.text: Which algorithm identifier, in which registry namespace, denotes the signature suite used, and what is its exact string or numeric value?
answer_data: identifier encoding form (name string, integer label, OID, IRI)

questions.text: Which parameters does the declared suite require in order to be unambiguous, and is each one present on the record?
answer_data: required parameter list for the suite

questions.text: Which curve, group or modulus size and which digest function and output length are bound to this signature?
answer_data: modulus or key size in bits

questions.text: How are absent, inherited or ambiguous algorithm parameters recorded so that they are never silently defaulted?
Is a pre-hash mode or context or domain-separation string in effect, and what is its value?

data_elements.name: Asserted algorithm identifier
data_elements.description: The signature algorithm identifier exactly as carried by the signature container or proof.

data_elements.name: Identifier registry namespace
data_elements.description: The registry or namespace that gives the identifier its meaning, so that a bare name such as ES256 is never ambiguous across registries.

data_elements.name: Suite parameter set
data_elements.description: Structured parameters that complete the suite: scheme variant, padding or encoding, salt length, pre-hash mode and context string.

data_elements.name: Digest algorithm and output length
data_elements.description: Registry-scoped digest algorithm identifier with its output length, including any truncation applied.

data_elements.name: Key, curve or group size
data_elements.description: Curve or group identifier and modulus or key size in bits for the verification key bound to the signature.

data_elements.name: Parameter completeness status
data_elements.description: Coded status stating whether the suite declaration is complete, incomplete, inherited or ambiguous, with the reason code when it is not complete.

findings.inline_only_rationale: Suite identification is a set of registry-governed identifiers and scalar parameters carried inline on the signature record. It has no standalone document form, and materialising it as a local artifact would fork the IANA, NIST and ETSI registry entries that this model only references and never maintains.

findings.name: Security strength, approval state and pinned algorithm policy
findings.description: Records the security strength the declared suite targets and the table that claim is made against, the approval state each governing authority assigns to it (approved, acceptable, deprecated, legacy-use, restricted, disallowed, or registry equivalents such as Recommended, No, Deprecated, Prohibited), any sunset or transition date, the time basis the sunset is evaluated against, and the exact policy snapshot pinned when the assessment was made. Disagreement between authorities is recorded, not resolved.

questions.text: What security strength in bits does the declared suite target, and against which strength table is that claim made?
What approval state does each governing authority assign to this suite, and do those authorities disagree?
answer_data: operation scope of the state (signature generation or verification)

questions.text: What sunset, deprecation or disallowance date applies, and relative to which time basis is it evaluated?
answer_data: time basis code (validation time or proof-of-existence time)

questions.text: Which exact policy snapshot version was pinned when this signature's algorithm state was assessed?

data_elements.name: Target security strength
data_elements.description: Security strength in bits attributed to the suite, with the reference table that supplies the mapping.

data_elements.name: Approval state per authority
data_elements.description: Coded transition or recommendation state assigned by a named authority, scoped to the operation (generation or verification).

data_elements.name: Policy authority reference
data_elements.description: Reference to the authority and document version that asserts an approval state or sunset date.

data_elements.name: Algorithm sunset date
data_elements.description: Date after which the suite is deprecated or disallowed under a named policy; a bare date, never used as an identifier.

data_elements.name: Pinned policy snapshot reference
data_elements.description: Reference to the immutable policy snapshot in force for this assessment, with its version and digest.

artifacts.name: Pinned algorithm policy snapshot
artifacts.description: An immutable, versioned capture of the algorithm-state catalogue in force when a signature's suite was assessed: approval states, strength mappings and sunset dates, together with the precedence order among authorities. The catalogue is published and maintained externally; this model records the pinned edition, its version and its digest.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Authoritative policy identifier issued by the publishing authority together with its version; where the publisher assigns none, a governed namespace IRI; only otherwise a UUID or ULID minted by the adopting Dimension and recorded with its minting authority. The snapshot digest is stored as integrity metadata and the publication date is descriptive; neither is the identifier.

layers.name: Agility, downgrade resistance and transition
layers.description: The controls and recorded state that keep a signature record meaningful as algorithms are constrained, combined or retired: verifier-side accepted-algorithm sets, signing randomness profile, and hybrid, composite and post-quantum migration state.

findings.name: Accepted-algorithm set and downgrade resistance
findings.description: Records the verifier-side accepted-algorithm set that governed a verification episode, where that set came from, whether the algorithm asserted in the signature container fell inside it, and the controls against algorithm confusion, reuse of one key across multiple algorithms, and acceptance of none or other non-signing algorithm values. The accepted set is a policy reference plus per-episode scalars; the deciding engine is external.

questions.text: Which accepted-algorithm set applied to this verification, and was it obtained from verifier policy or from the signature container?
answer_data: policy source code (verifier policy or container-asserted)

questions.text: Did the algorithm asserted in the container fall inside the accepted set, and if not, which reason code is recorded?
Is the verification key bound to exactly one algorithm, and was that binding actually checked during the episode?
How are unauthenticated, none or otherwise non-signing algorithm values handled and recorded?

data_elements.name: Accepted algorithm set
data_elements.description: The identifiers a verifier was permitted to accept for this episode, recorded as a reference into the pinned policy snapshot plus any episode-local narrowing.

data_elements.name: Container-asserted algorithm
data_elements.description: The algorithm value carried by the signature container, held separately from the accepted set so that the two can be compared.

data_elements.name: Downgrade or confusion indicator
data_elements.description: Coded indicator recording a downgrade attempt, algorithm-confusion condition or unauthenticated algorithm value observed for this signature.

data_elements.name: Key to algorithm binding reference
data_elements.description: Reference to the declaration that binds the verification key to one and only one algorithm, held in the verification-method model.

findings.inline_only_rationale: The accepted-algorithm set is recorded as a reference into the externally published policy snapshot plus a small number of per-episode coded values. Creating a separate local artifact would produce a second, competing copy of a policy that the adopting Dimension's configuration store already holds as the record of authority.

findings.name: Randomized, deterministic and hedged signing profile
findings.description: Records whether the signature was produced with a randomized, deterministic or hedged per-message secret process, on what basis that claim rests, and the explicit limitation that deterministic and randomized signatures of the same suite are indistinguishable to a verifier holding only the signature value.

questions.text: Which per-message randomness mode does the signer claim - randomized, deterministic or hedged - and for which suite?
What evidence supports the randomness-mode claim, given that a verifier cannot infer it from the signature value?
answer_data: evidence type (device attestation, signer declaration, test vector, none)

questions.text: What operational risk is recorded when the randomness mode is unknown or the signer's entropy source is unattested?
Does the recorded mode change the bytes a verifier must process or the identifier it must accept?

data_elements.name: Per-message randomness mode
data_elements.description: Coded claim that signing used a randomized, deterministic or hedged per-message secret process.

data_elements.name: Randomness-mode evidence reference
data_elements.description: Reference to any external evidence supporting the mode claim, such as a device attestation or a signer declaration.

data_elements.name: Verifier observability flag
data_elements.description: Boolean stating whether the mode is derivable by the verifier from the signature alone; false for the classical DSA and ECDSA families.

findings.inline_only_rationale: The randomness profile is a small set of coded claims plus references to evidence held elsewhere. Materialising it as an artifact would suggest a verifier-side proof of the signer's nonce derivation that the deterministic-signature specification explicitly states does not exist, since such signatures remain indistinguishable from randomized ones.

findings.name: Hybrid, composite and post-quantum transition state
findings.description: Records multi-algorithm proofs - composite or parallel hybrid - their ordered component algorithms and parameter sets, the combination rule that governs the overall result, the security property the combination claims relative to its components, and the post-quantum migration state assigned by a named policy and jurisdiction. No universal transition deadline is asserted.

questions.text: Which component algorithms make up this composite or hybrid proof, and under which composite identifier are they combined?
What combination rule governs the overall result - must every component verify, or is a subset sufficient?
Which post-quantum migration state is recorded for this signature, and which named policy and jurisdiction assign it?
Which security property does the combination claim, and is that property weaker than the property of its strongest component?
answer_data: claimed security property (for example EUF-CMA or SUF-CMA)

data_elements.name: Composite or hybrid identifier
data_elements.description: Registry-scoped identifier for the combined construction, distinct from the identifiers of its components.

data_elements.name: Component algorithm list
data_elements.description: Ordered list of component suites with their parameter sets and individual result slots.

data_elements.name: Combination rule
data_elements.description: Coded rule stating how component results combine; the default for composite constructions is that every component must verify.

data_elements.name: Post-quantum migration state
data_elements.description: Coded migration state relative to a named transition policy, always carried with the policy and jurisdiction reference.

findings.inline_only_rationale: Composite structure, combination rule and migration state are coded values and ordered references over identifiers that other registries own. The component signature values themselves live in the signature container held by the host record, so there is nothing here that has an independent document form.

bundles.name: Verification context, verdicts and evidence
bundles.description: The context that makes a recorded verification outcome reproducible and honestly bounded: the inputs and time basis it consumed, the verifier and tooling that produced it, the structured outcome vocabulary it uses, and the separation of the distinct validity dimensions it reports.
bundles.rationale: Recording an outcome without its inputs, time basis, policy pin and producing tool makes the outcome unfalsifiable. ETSI supplies a normative three-valued indication with justifying sub-indications and a report structure, W3C supplies a proof-purpose and verification-result model, and CMS and TSP supply the claimed-time versus proof-of-existence distinction, so this concern is grounded and separable from the algorithm declaration it consumes.

layers.name: Verification inputs and reproducibility pins
layers.description: What a verification episode consumed and who produced it: covered content and canonicalisation, verification-method reference, validation time and time basis, claimed signing time against proof of existence, and the verifier, tool and evidence bindings that let a verdict be re-derived or challenged.

findings.name: Verification input set, validation time and time claims
findings.description: Records the complete input set consumed by a verification episode: the covered byte sequence and the ordered canonicalisation or transform chain that produced it, the resolved verification-method reference, the validation time and the basis on which it was chosen, the validation material supplied versus fetched, and the claimed signing time held explicitly as an untrusted claim alongside any proof-of-existence reference that supports it.

questions.text: Exactly which byte sequence was covered by the signature, and through which canonicalisation or transform chain was it derived?
answer_data: covered-content digest with its digest algorithm

questions.text: Which validation time was used for this episode, and why was that time chosen rather than another?
answer_data: validation time as RFC 3339 with offset
time basis code (current time, claimed signing time, proof-of-existence time)

questions.text: What signing time does the signature claim, and what external evidence, if any, supports that claim?
Which validation material was supplied to the episode rather than fetched, and is it complete for the chosen validation time?
Which verification method or key identifier was resolved for this episode, and in which reference form?
answer_data: reference form (URI, key identifier, certificate reference)

data_elements.name: Covered content digest
data_elements.description: Digest over the exact byte sequence the signature covers, always stored with the naming of its digest algorithm.

data_elements.name: Canonicalisation and transform chain
data_elements.description: Ordered identifiers of the canonicalisation or transform steps applied before signing, preserved verbatim and never re-applied at storage time.

data_elements.name: Validation time and basis
data_elements.description: The time at which validation constraints were evaluated, with the coded basis on which that time was selected.

data_elements.name: Claimed signing time
data_elements.description: The time the signer asserts the signature was created; an untrusted claim unless an external proof of existence supports it.

data_elements.name: Proof-of-existence reference
data_elements.description: Reference to a time-stamp token or equivalent evidence showing the signature existed before a stated time.

data_elements.name: Verification method reference
data_elements.description: Reference to the verification method or key used, resolved in the model that owns it.

findings.inline_only_rationale: Every input here is a scalar or a reference into an object that a neighbouring model owns: the covered payload belongs to the host record, the verification method to the key model, and the time-stamp token to the proof-of-existence model. Copying any of them into a local artifact would create a second, drifting record of authority.

findings.name: Verifier, tool and evidence pinning
findings.description: Records who or what produced a verdict, with which software identity, version and configuration, at which observation or ingestion time as distinct from the validation time it was computed for, and which externally produced validation report the verdict is bound to and by which digest. It also records what must be held constant to re-derive the verdict and what is known to be non-reproducible.

questions.text: Which verifying party, and which tool, library and version, produced this verdict?
When was the verdict observed and ingested, as distinct from the validation time it was computed for?
Which validation report or evidence object is this verdict bound to, and how is that binding integrity-protected?
What must be held constant to reproduce this verdict, and which factors are known to be non-reproducible?

data_elements.name: Verifying party reference
data_elements.description: Reference to the party or service that produced the verdict; anonymous verdicts are not admissible.

data_elements.name: Tool and version pin
data_elements.description: Identifier, version and configuration of the software that computed the verdict.

data_elements.name: Observation or ingestion time
data_elements.description: When the verdict was observed and stored by the adopting Dimension, held separately from validation time and claimed signing time.

data_elements.name: Evidence digest
data_elements.description: Digest binding the verdict to the referenced validation report or evidence object, stored with its digest algorithm.

data_elements.name: Reproducibility status
data_elements.description: Coded statement of whether the verdict can be re-derived from the pinned inputs, and why not where it cannot.

artifacts.name: Referenced signature validation report
artifacts.description: A structured report, produced by an external validation application, that enumerates each validation check and constraint, the status it produced, the justification for that status, and the validation objects used such as trust anchors, revocation data and time-stamps. This model records the reference, identity and digest of the report; it neither produces the report nor owns the producing system's audit trail.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Report identifier assigned by the producing validation application as the authoritative master system; failing that, a governed IRI in the producer's namespace; only otherwise a UUID or ULID minted by the adopting Dimension with its minting authority recorded. The report digest is integrity metadata and the report date is descriptive; neither serves as the identifier.

layers.name: Structured verdicts and dimension separation
layers.description: What a recorded outcome may say and what it may never imply: a closed outcome vocabulary with mandatory machine-readable reasons, and independent reporting of cryptographic validity, trust path, identity binding, authorization, proof purpose, qualification and legal effect.

findings.name: Structured verification outcomes and machine-readable reasons
findings.description: Defines the closed outcome vocabulary a recorded verdict may take - valid, invalid, indeterminate, unsupported, malformed, policy-rejected and evidence-incomplete - each carrying at least one machine-readable reason code when it is not valid, together with versioned mappings to external status vocabularies and explicit marking of where those mappings lose information.

questions.text: Which outcome value does this verdict carry, and from which closed vocabulary version is it drawn?
Which machine-readable reason codes justify the outcome, and is at least one recorded for every non-valid result?
How does each local outcome map onto external status vocabularies, and where is that mapping lossy?
What distinguishes indeterminate and evidence-incomplete from invalid, and what would resolve them?
How is an unsupported algorithm distinguished from a malformed structure in the recorded outcome?

data_elements.name: Outcome value
data_elements.description: The single coded outcome of the recorded verdict, drawn from the closed vocabulary.

data_elements.name: Reason codes
data_elements.description: Machine-readable justifications for the outcome; at least one is required whenever the outcome is anything other than valid.

data_elements.name: Human-readable message
data_elements.description: Optional narrative accompanying the codes; never a substitute for a reason code.

data_elements.name: External vocabulary mapping
data_elements.description: Versioned mapping entries from local outcome and reason codes to external status indications and sub-indications, each marked lossless or lossy.

artifacts.name: Verdict outcome and reason-code vocabulary
artifacts.description: A governed, versioned code list defining the permitted outcome values, the reason codes available under each, and the versioned mappings from those codes to external status vocabularies with lossiness marked. It is the term set a verdict record cites; it does not decide any verdict.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Identifier issued by the maintaining authority where one exists; where the adopting Dimension maintains the vocabulary, a governed namespace IRI plus a semantic version; a UUID or ULID only as a last resort. Editions are disambiguated by version, never by release date.

findings.name: Separation of validity dimensions in a verdict
findings.description: Requires each verdict to report cryptographic primitive validity, trust-path outcome, identity binding, authorization, proof purpose, qualification and legal effect as independent dimensions, each with its own outcome, reason code and owning authority, and each explicitly marked not-assessed when it was not evaluated. A successful primitive check never sets any other dimension, and any single summary flag must declare the derivation rule and the information it discards.

questions.text: Which validity dimensions are reported for this verdict, and which are explicitly marked not assessed?
Which model or authority owns the determination of each dimension, and is that determination referenced rather than recomputed here?
For which declared proof purpose was the signature accepted, and does it match the purpose the verification method authorises?
answer_data: purpose match result with reason code

questions.text: Which rule governs deriving a single summary flag, and what information does that derivation discard?
Where is any qualification or legal-effect determination recorded, and under which jurisdiction and instrument was it made?

data_elements.name: Per-dimension outcomes
data_elements.description: One entry per validity dimension, each carrying its own outcome code, reason codes and not-assessed marker.

data_elements.name: Declared proof purpose
data_elements.description: The purpose the proof declares, used to prevent a proof being applied to a purpose it was not created for.

data_elements.name: Dimension determination authority
data_elements.description: Reference to the external model, authority or instrument that determined a given non-cryptographic dimension.

data_elements.name: Derived summary flag
data_elements.description: Optional single boolean derived for constrained consumers; admissible only with its derivation rule and loss note recorded.

findings.inline_only_rationale: Each dimension outcome is a coded reference to a determination that an external model or authority makes. Holding these as local artifacts would create a competing record of determinations this model does not perform, and would blur the boundary it exists to keep sharp.

functions.name: Resolve a declared algorithm identifier into a complete suite descriptor
functions.description: Normalises a container-asserted algorithm identifier against its registry namespace and expands it into the full parameter set required for unambiguous verification, recording any parameter that is absent, inherited or ambiguous as an explicit gap.
inputs: asserted algorithm identifier and registry namespace
any inherited or externally supplied parameters
preconditions: a signature record exists carrying at least one asserted algorithm identifier
the registry alignment for that namespace is declared
effects: writes the normalised suite descriptor and completeness status onto the signature record
records unresolved parameters as a gap instead of applying a silent default
performs no cryptographic operation and changes no signature bytes

functions.name: Classify approval state and security strength against a pinned policy
functions.description: Compares a normalised suite descriptor with a pinned algorithm policy snapshot and records the approval state, security-strength assessment and sunset comparison for each governing authority, preserving disagreements rather than resolving them.
preconditions: a policy snapshot is pinned with its version and digest
an evaluation time basis has been chosen and recorded
effects: writes a non-enforcing classification onto the record
records divergence between authorities without selecting a winner
does not accept or reject the signature; acceptance remains a decision of the adopting Dimension's policy engine

functions.name: Compare the container-asserted algorithm with the accepted-algorithm set
functions.description: Records whether the algorithm asserted in the signature container fell inside the verifier-side accepted set, whether the key-to-algorithm binding was checked, and whether an unauthenticated or non-signing algorithm value was present.
inputs: accepted algorithm set reference and version
preconditions: an accepted-algorithm set is referenced with its policy source recorded
effects: records the comparison result and its reason code
flags cases where algorithm selection came from the container rather than verifier policy
raises no enforcement action and blocks nothing

functions.name: Pin the verification context for an episode
functions.description: Freezes the inputs that a later re-derivation must reproduce: validation time and its basis, the policy and vocabulary versions in force, the verifier and tool identity, and the references to supplied validation material.
inputs: policy snapshot and vocabulary version references
preconditions: the signature record and its covered-content digest are resolvable
the covered-content digest algorithm is named
effects: creates an immutable context that later verdicts cite
records observation or ingestion time separately from validation time
does not fetch, validate or evaluate any referenced material

functions.name: Record a structured, dimension-separated verdict with evidence references
functions.description: Stores an outcome produced by an external verifier, together with its reason codes, independent per-dimension outcomes, and the digest-bound reference to the validation report or other evidence that justifies it.
inputs: outcome value and reason codes from the external verifier
evidence or report reference with digest
outputs: list of dimensions explicitly not assessed
preconditions: the outcome vocabulary version is declared
the producing verifier and tool version are known
effects: stores the verdict without recomputing the underlying cryptographic check
marks unassessed dimensions explicitly instead of defaulting them to valid
binds referenced evidence by digest while leaving the producing system's execution and audit trail entirely outside this model

functions.name: Supersede a prior verdict on re-validation
functions.description: Appends a new verdict that cites its predecessor and the reason for re-validation, and records the drift between the two pinned policy snapshots so that a changed result can be attributed to policy movement rather than to the signature.
outputs: superseding verdict record linked to its predecessor
preconditions: a prior verdict exists and is immutable
the new policy pin and vocabulary version are recorded
effects: appends rather than overwrites, preserving the earlier verdict and its evidence binding
records algorithm-state drift between the two policy pins
leaves disposition of the superseded record to the retention rule and to the owning retention policy

composition.target: WM-XCT-006 (parent cryptographic-context model in the XCT family)
composition.purpose: This mixin is registered beneath WM-XCT-006 and specialises its framing for signatures and proofs only. Generic cryptographic-context identity, authority and conflict machinery stays in the parent; only signature-specific suite declaration, agility posture and verdict semantics are elaborated here.

Carry the verification-method or key reference, its algorithm binding and subject-specific parameters. Key generation, custody, rotation, revocation and device assurance remain the target's lifecycle and are not reproduced here.

composition.target: Certificate trust-path and revocation validation model
composition.purpose: Reference the trust-path determination and its reason codes as one reported dimension of a verdict. Path construction, revocation retrieval and trusted-list evaluation are the target's operational functions.

Reference time-stamp tokens as external evidence supporting a signing-time claim and as the time basis for sunset comparison. Token issuance, TSA policy and time-source traceability stay with the target.

composition.target: Verification service execution and audit-record model
composition.purpose: Record verifier identity, tool version and validation-report references as provenance. Executing verification, enforcing acceptance and maintaining the audit trail belong exclusively to the target.

composition.target: Signed host record or artifact model
composition.purpose: Attach signature and proof context to any host record or artifact. The host retains its own content model, business lifecycle and retention execution; this mixin adds only the signature, algorithm-policy and verdict facets.

composition.target: NIST digital-signature algorithm catalogue (FIPS 186-5 and FIPS 204)
composition.purpose: Align local suite descriptors with NIST-approved algorithm names and parameter sets. NIST retains definition and approval authority; alignment is a mapping and is never recorded as a conformance claim.

composition.target: IANA COSE and JOSE algorithm registries
composition.purpose: Bind registry-scoped identifiers together with their recommendation or implementation-requirement states. The registries remain the change-controlled source and are referenced, never mirrored or re-minted.

composition.target: ETSI AdES validation-semantics profile (EN 319 102-1 and TS 119 102-2)
composition.purpose: Map local outcome and reason codes onto ETSI status indications and sub-indications, marking lossy mappings explicitly. The validation procedure itself is executed under the target's rules, not here.

Reference an external qualification or legal-effect determination with its jurisdiction, instrument and date as separate reported dimensions. The determination is made under the target's authority and is never inferred from a cryptographic result.
Reference a named migration policy and jurisdiction that assigns the recorded migration state. Setting transition dates, mandates and compliance deadlines belongs to that policy, not to this model.

owner_package_requirements: Name a single accountable owner for the pinned algorithm-policy snapshot and for the outcome and reason-code vocabulary before any record is created.

Declare which external algorithm catalogues (NIST, IANA, ETSI, national) are authoritative for this Dimension and in what precedence order when they disagree; disagreement must be recorded, not silently resolved.
Declare the bound referenced models that own key lifecycle, trust-path validation, time-stamping, verification execution and legal qualification; adoption is incomplete without those bindings.
Publish the retention, supersession and tombstone rule for verdict records, verification contexts and pinned policy snapshots before the first verdict is stored.
dimension.namespace_guidance: Local identifiers live under the adopting Dimension's namespace and always begin with the model's own prefix. External algorithm identifiers keep their originating registry namespace verbatim - OID arc, COSE integer label, JOSE algorithm name, W3C cryptosuite string - and are never re-minted locally. Every recorded identifier carries its namespace so that a bare name such as EdDSA or ES256 is never ambiguous across registries, and no identifier contains a date-like component.
registry_links: IANA JSON Web Signature and Encryption Algorithms registry: https://www.iana.org/assignments/jose/jose.xhtml

canonicalization_rules: Record algorithm identifiers exactly as issued by their registry, together with the namespace; normalise case only where the registry itself declares case-insensitivity.

Record the canonicalisation or transform chain applied to the covered content as an ordered list and preserve it verbatim; never re-canonicalise signed bytes when storing, projecting or re-serialising the record.
Express all time values as RFC 3339 with seconds and an explicit offset or Z; never normalise a claimed signing time into the verifier's local zone or drop its original offset.
Store digests with an explicitly named digest algorithm; a digest without its algorithm is treated as incomplete evidence.
patch_rules: Verdicts, verification contexts and policy pins are append-only: correction is by a superseding record citing its predecessor and a reason, never by in-place edit.
A change to the asserted algorithm identifier, the suite parameter set or the covered-content digest is breaking and requires a new signature-context record rather than a patch.
Reason codes may be added within a vocabulary version; removing a code or changing its meaning requires a new vocabulary version and a new mapping edition.
Annotations that carry no semantics - labels, human-readable messages, additional external mappings - may be updated in place provided the actor, reason and timestamp are recorded.
compatibility_rules: Adding an outcome value or reason code is a minor change; changing the meaning of an existing outcome value, or narrowing the reported dimension set, is breaking.
A consumer that cannot interpret a reason code must degrade to the outcome value and mark the reason as unrecognised; it must never degrade toward valid.
Alignment mappings to external vocabularies are versioned independently of the local vocabulary and may be marked lossy without constituting a breaking change.
A summary boolean derived from the dimension set is a projection, not an interface contract; consumers must not treat its absence as a failure.

identity_priority: Authoritative master-system identifier: the identifier assigned by the system of record that issued the artifact - for example the validation application's report identifier or the publishing authority's policy-snapshot identifier.

Governed global identifier or IRI: a registry-controlled identifier such as an algorithm OID, a COSE or JOSE registry entry, a W3C cryptosuite string, or a namespace IRI for a Dimension-maintained vocabulary.
UUID or ULID minted by the adopting Dimension, used only when neither of the above exists, and always recorded together with the minting authority.
A date, a version string alone, or a content digest is never an identifier; digests are recorded as integrity metadata alongside the identifier, never in place of it.
artifact_rules.timestamp_rule: All time values use RFC 3339 with seconds precision and an explicit UTC offset or Z. Event time - claimed signing time, time-stamp token time, validation time, policy sunset date - is recorded separately from observation or ingestion time, which is when the verdict or evidence was seen and stored by the adopting Dimension. Where these differ, both are stored, neither is derived from the other, and the time basis used for any sunset or revocation comparison is stated explicitly.
artifact_rules.serial_naming_rule: Serial artifacts such as validation reports and policy snapshots are named by stable artifact identity plus a monotonically increasing sequence or semantic version, never by date alone. The sequence is scoped to the issuing authority, and a superseded member keeps its original name so that earlier references remain resolvable.
artifact_rules.integrity_rule: Every referenced artifact carries a digest with an explicitly named digest algorithm together with the retrieval reference used. If that digest algorithm is itself deprecated or disallowed under the pinned policy, or if the reference no longer dereferences, the binding is recorded as evidence-incomplete rather than silently accepted.

policies: A successful cryptographic primitive check never sets the trust-path, identity-binding, authorization, proof-purpose, qualification or legal-effect dimensions; any dimension not evaluated is recorded as not assessed.

Accepted algorithms are determined by verifier-side policy, never by the algorithm asserted in the signature container; a container-asserted algorithm outside the accepted set is recorded as policy-rejected with a reason code, and unauthenticated or none values are never accepted implicitly.
Claimed signing time is untrusted unless an external proof-of-existence reference supports it; every sunset, expiry or revocation comparison states which time basis it used.
No conformance claim to an external standard is recorded without an evidence reference; alignments are recorded as versioned mappings, and sources in draft status are marked as draft.

This model records algorithm policy state and verdicts as data. It never executes verification, never enforces acceptance or rejection, and never maintains the verifying system's audit trail; each of those resolves to a referenced model.

read: Reading a verdict always returns its pinned verification context, policy snapshot reference, vocabulary version and time basis; a verdict is never served detached from these.
A bare outcome value must not be exposed without its reason codes and its per-dimension outcome set, including the not-assessed markers.
Algorithm descriptors may be read independently of any verdict, for inventory and agility reporting.
create: A signature-context record is created only with at least one asserted algorithm identifier, its registry namespace, and the covered-content digest with its named digest algorithm.
A verdict is created only against an already pinned verification context and an explicitly declared outcome vocabulary version.
Creating a verdict requires the producing verifier's identity and tool version; anonymous or unattributed verdicts are rejected at creation.
A policy snapshot reference is created only with its version and digest; an unpinned or floating policy reference is not admissible.
update: Algorithm descriptors, covered-content bindings and verification contexts are immutable after creation; any change means a new record.
Verdicts are superseded rather than edited, with the superseding record citing its predecessor, the reason for re-validation and the policy-pin drift.
Only non-semantic annotations - labels, human-readable messages, additional external mappings - may be updated in place, and only with actor, reason and RFC 3339 timestamp recorded.
delete: Records of this model are not hard-deleted by default. A superseded or withdrawn verdict is tombstoned: its identifier, outcome code, policy pin reference, verifier reference and withdrawal reason are retained, while free-text messages and payload references may be redacted.

Minimum retention is the longer of the evidence-retention period stated by the pinned policy and the retention required by the host record that carries the signature; this model defines no absolute retention period of its own.

Execution of deletion, redaction and legal-hold release is owned by the adopting Dimension's retention policy together with the host-record model and the verification-service model. This model contributes only the tombstone shape, the retention dependency and the requirement that a deletion event records its authorising instrument, actor and timestamp.

Referenced external artifacts - validation reports, time-stamp tokens, policy snapshots - are never deleted through this model. Only the local reference and its digest are removed, and the resulting loss of dereferenceability is recorded as evidence-incomplete on any verdict that depended on it.

roles.name: Signature Context Steward
responsibilities: Maintain the completeness and accuracy of algorithm descriptors and covered-content bindings.
Ensure absent, inherited or ambiguous parameters are recorded as explicit gaps rather than defaulted.
Reject creation of signature-context records lacking a namespace-qualified algorithm identifier or a named digest algorithm.

roles.name: Cryptographic Policy Curator
responsibilities: Pin, version and publish algorithm-policy snapshots and the precedence order among authorities.
Record disagreements between NIST, IANA, ETSI and national catalogues without silently resolving them.
Track deprecation, sunset and post-quantum migration state per named policy and jurisdiction, and mark draft sources as draft.

roles.name: Verification Evidence Custodian
responsibilities: Bind verdicts to externally produced validation reports by identifier and digest.
Detect and record loss of dereferenceability or digest-algorithm deprecation in referenced evidence.
Ensure verifier identity, tool version and observation time are present on every stored verdict.

roles.name: Vocabulary and Interoperability Maintainer
responsibilities: Own the outcome and reason-code vocabulary and its versioning.
Maintain mappings to external status vocabularies and mark lossy mappings explicitly.
Review consumer degradation behaviour so that unknown codes never degrade toward valid.

roles.name: Dimension Data Owner
responsibilities: Approve the adoption bindings to referenced models for key lifecycle, trust path, timestamping, verification execution and qualification.
Own retention, access and disposition decisions for records of this model.
Authorise exceptions to the default access rule and record the authorising instrument.

access.default_rule: Read access to signature-context records, algorithm descriptors and verdicts follows the access already granted on the host record they annotate; write access is limited to the stewarding roles named for the relevant finding.
exceptions: Verdicts revealing an exploitable weakness - for example a suite classified as disallowed on a signature still in production use - are restricted to security roles until the record is remediated or superseded.

Referenced validation reports may embed signer personal data or business-confidential payload references, so artifact-scope access may be narrower than the finding-scope access that governs the surrounding verdict.
Draft or unpinned policy snapshots are readable only by the Cryptographic Policy Curator role until they are pinned and versioned.
Bulk export of algorithm descriptors across a corpus is treated as an agility-inventory disclosure and requires Dimension Data Owner approval.
audit_requirements: Every supersession, tombstone, redaction and vocabulary version change records the actor, the reason and an RFC 3339 timestamp with an explicit offset on the record itself.

Where a verdict read is used to make an external acceptance decision, the reader, purpose and verdict identifier are recorded by the consuming system's audit facility; this model supplies the verdict identifier and policy pin for that record but does not own or write the audit trail.
Access-exception grants record the authorising instrument and an expiry, and are reviewed when the pinned policy snapshot changes.

read_order: AGENTS.md first: model name, type, specification, storage type, interface and process URLs, plus the pinned policy and vocabulary versions currently in force.
Model scope statement, out-of-scope list and boundary notes, so that no capability owned by a referenced model is invoked locally.
The composition ledger, to resolve which model owns key lifecycle, trust path, timestamping, verification execution and qualification before any verdict is read or written.
The bundle, layer and finding structure, then the finding-level questions relevant to the task at hand.

coverage.claim: This structure covers the signature and proof context surface - suite declaration, algorithm policy state, agility and transition posture, verification inputs and reproducibility, and structured dimension-separated verdicts - as defined by NIST signature and transition guidance, the IANA COSE and JOSE algorithm registries, IETF signature-format and best-current-practice documents, ETSI AdES validation semantics and W3C Data Integrity proof semantics. It is falsifiable: every node cites a retrievable source, draft sources are marked as draft, and gaps, conflicts and regional assumptions are listed rather than smoothed over. No claim of universal or metaphysical completeness is made.

checklist.notes: Algorithm identifiers are namespace-qualified so a bare name is never ambiguous; artifact identity follows master-system identifier, then governed IRI, then UUID or ULID, with dates and digests explicitly excluded as identifiers.

Signature-context records and verification contexts are immutable; verdicts are append-only with supersession and recorded policy-pin drift. Key, certificate and device lifecycle is deliberately referenced, not modelled.
Composite component relations, proof-purpose to verification-method relations, predecessor links between verdicts and dimension-owner references are modelled as links rather than copies.

Validation time and its basis, claimed signing time, proof-of-existence reference, sunset date and observation or ingestion time are separate elements, all RFC 3339 with seconds and an explicit offset.
Verifier identity, tool and version, configuration pin, policy snapshot version and digest-bound evidence reference are required for every verdict; anonymous verdicts are rejected at creation.
Five named roles carry responsibilities, and a per-dimension authority element records which external model or instrument determined each non-cryptographic dimension.

A closed outcome vocabulary with mandatory reason codes, parameter-completeness status, accepted-set comparison and reproducibility status define validation of the record itself; cryptographic execution stays external.

Default rule inherits host-record access with narrower artifact scope; four exception classes cover exploitable-weakness disclosure, personal data in reports, unpinned policy drafts and bulk agility inventory.

Tombstone shape retains identifier, outcome, policy pin, verifier and withdrawal reason; retention is the longer of pinned-policy and host-record requirements, and deletion execution is delegated to the adopting Dimension, host-record and verification-service models.
Registry-scoped identifiers, versioned mappings to external status vocabularies with explicit lossiness marking, and a degrade-safe rule that unknown reason codes never degrade toward valid.

Approval state per authority with operation scope, security strength with its reference table, sunset date with time basis, verifier-side accepted set, and hybrid, composite and post-quantum migration state.

Downgrade, algorithm confusion, key-to-algorithm binding, unauthenticated algorithm values, weak or truncated digests and unattested randomness are all recordable conditions; enforcement is explicitly excluded.
Security strength is expressed in bits with the strength table reference, its version, and a claimed-versus-assessed flag so an unverified vendor claim is distinguishable.
Evidence completeness, digest-algorithm deprecation, dereferenceability loss and reproducibility limits are first-class recorded states rather than silent failures.

Signer personal data inside referenced validation reports and payload references is handled only at the access layer. No data-minimisation model exists for selective-disclosure or zero-knowledge proof forms, which would need a sibling model.

known_omissions: Selective-disclosure and zero-knowledge proof systems, including derived-proof and unlinkability semantics, are accommodated only by the generic outcome and dimension slots; their predicate and derivation semantics are not modelled.
Remote-attestation evidence appraisal, where an appraisal policy rather than a signature check drives the verdict, is out of scope and would require a sibling model.

National and regional algorithm catalogues such as SOG-IS agreed mechanisms, BSI TR-02102, ANSSI guidance and the SM2 and SM3 family are not enumerated; only the precedence and disagreement-recording mechanism is provided.
Concrete algorithm object identifiers, parameter tables and curve definitions are deliberately not reproduced; they remain in the referenced registries and standards.
Threshold, multi-party and aggregate signature schemes have no dedicated combination-rule vocabulary beyond the generic composite rule, and their partial-participation semantics are unmodelled.
Long-term archival re-signing and evidence-record augmentation are reachable only through proof-of-existence references; the augmentation lifecycle itself is not modelled.
Signature-creation-time policy - what a signer was permitted to sign and with which device - is out of scope; only the resulting declared parameters are recorded.
conflicts: The IANA JOSE registry marks the EdDSA algorithm name Deprecated in favour of separate Ed25519 and Ed448 entries, while other profiles and the COSE registry continue to carry EdDSA-labelled entries; a bare algorithm name is therefore not portable across registries and must always be namespace-qualified.

NIST SP 800-131A Rev. 3 remains an initial public draft dated 21 October 2024 proposing retirement of DSA signature generation and of SHA-1 and 224-bit hash functions, while Rev. 2 of March 2019 is the final publication in force; a policy pin must state which one it cites.

NIST IR 8547 is an initial public draft dated 12 November 2024 with indicative deprecation around 2030 and disallowance by 2035, whereas ETSI and national catalogues publish different sunset dates; no universal transition date is asserted by this model.

FIPS 186-5 retains DSA for verification of existing signatures only, while some deployed ecosystems still generate DSA signatures, so approval state differs by operation and must be recorded separately for generation and verification.

The ETSI three-valued indication of TOTAL-PASSED, INDETERMINATE and TOTAL-FAILED has no lossless mapping onto the W3C Data Integrity boolean verification result; indeterminate collapses to false unless the mapping is explicitly marked lossy.

The COSE registry expresses identifier state as Recommended Yes, No or Deprecated, while the JOSE registry uses Required, Recommended, Optional, Deprecated and Prohibited; the two state vocabularies are not interchangeable and must be mapped, not merged.
Composite ML-DSA constructions achieve EUF-CMA rather than the SUF-CMA property of pure ML-DSA, so a hybrid is not automatically stronger than its strongest component on every security property.
regional_assumptions: FIPS approval states and NIST transition dates are United States federal policy and are not globally binding; they are recorded as one policy authority among several with an explicit precedence order.

Signature qualification, trusted-list membership and legal effect are European Union constructs; outside that jurisdiction those dimension slots remain not assessed unless a local instrument is referenced.
Draft post-quantum transition dates are treated as indicative only; an adopting Dimension in another jurisdiction pins its own national roadmap as the governing policy.
The model assumes offset-bearing timestamps are available; where local civil time is required by regulation it is a derived presentation, never the stored value.
Where a Dimension operates under a national cryptographic catalogue not enumerated here, the precedence mechanism applies but the catalogue itself must be registered before adoption.
adversarial_checks: Counterexample test - a signature whose primitive check succeeds but whose verification method is not authorised for the declared proof purpose must not be recordable as overall valid; the mandatory dimension set forces a purpose-mismatch outcome with its own reason code.

Downgrade test - a container asserting none, or an HMAC algorithm presented against an RSA public key, must be recorded as policy-rejected with a key-to-algorithm binding reason, because the accepted set is verifier-side and never taken from the container.

Time test - a signature claiming a signing time inside the certificate validity window but carrying no proof-of-existence reference cannot resolve sunset or revocation questions; the correct outcome is indeterminate or evidence-incomplete, never valid.

Observability test - the model must not permit deterministic to be recorded as a verified fact inferred from the signature value alone, since deterministic and randomized signatures of the same suite are indistinguishable to a verifier.
Composite test - a proof whose post-quantum component verifies while its classical component fails must be recorded as invalid; no partial or degraded pass state exists in the outcome vocabulary.
Staleness test - reusing a verdict recorded under an earlier policy pin after the suite's sunset date must surface as policy-pin drift on a superseding record, not as a fresh valid result.

Boundary test - no bundle, layer, finding or function of this model executes verification, enforces acceptance, evaluates a trust path, or writes the verifying system's audit trail; every such capability resolves to a REFERENCE link with the target named.

Ambiguity test - a suite declaration missing a required parameter must yield an explicit incomplete status with a reason code; it must never be completed by applying an implementation default and then reported as valid.
